analysis.one_liner: Creates a government health insurance program covering every U.S. resident, financed by new taxes on individuals, employers, and corporations.
analysis.headline: The universal 'Mediplan' health insurance bill never advanced past subcommittee referral in the House and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have extended Medicare-style health coverage to every U.S. resident, enrolling people automatically at birth and issuing a national health card. Everyone would get Medicare benefits with a $500 yearly deductible and a $2,500 cap on total out-of-pocket costs; children, pregnant women, and people below the poverty line would pay nothing and get extra services like prescription drugs, eyeglasses, and well-child care. It would be paid for with new taxes: up to $1,000 plus 2% of income above $16,000 on individuals, a 2% tax on corporations, and a payroll tax on employers of 40 cents per hour or 10% of wages.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident gains guaranteed health coverage, with the largest gains for the uninsured, children, pregnant women, and low-income people, who would owe nothing out of pocket and receive benefits Medicare does not cover. People in between the poverty line and twice it would owe reduced cost-sharing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: All residents, especially the uninsured and poor

how_it_helps.text: Makes every U.S. resident eligible for a new Mediplan program with the same benefits as Medicare, with automatic enrollment at birth and a Mediplan card for claims.
Caps each individual's total yearly out-of-pocket costs (deductibles, coinsurance, copayments) at $2,500, after a $500 deductible.

Charges children under 23, pregnant women, and people below the federal poverty line no deductible, coinsurance, or copayments, and gives them extra benefits including outpatient prescription drugs, eyeglasses and hearing aids, well-child preventive care, and full pregnancy-related care including postnatal family planning.
Phases out cost-sharing for people with incomes between the poverty level and twice that level, in proportion to how far above poverty their income is.
Bars extra billing: doctors and hospitals would be paid only on an assignment basis, so patients could not be billed above the program's allowed charge.
Redirects state Medicaid spending into the program through maintenance-of-effort payments and folds Medicaid, federal employee, and military dependent coverage into Mediplan to avoid duplication.
Protects people who already have extra benefits from employer group health plans by requiring those plans to keep providing them, enforceable with triple damages.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals would pay a new tax reaching about $1,000 a year at higher incomes plus 2% of income over $16,000; corporations and tax-exempt organizations would pay 2% of alternative minimum taxable income; employers would pay 40 cents per hour (10% of wages for salaried workers) per employee, capped at $800 per employee.

drawbacks.text: The financing is a broad new tax burden: a basic tax of up to $1,000 per person (12.5% of income over $8,000), a 2% supplemental tax on income over $16,000, a 2% corporate tax, and a new employer payroll tax, with no offsetting cuts elsewhere.
Most beneficiaries would still face a $500 deductible and up to $2,500 in annual cost-sharing, so the plan is not first-dollar coverage for working adults.
Pregnancy services would require prior authorization from peer review organizations except for routine services, adding an approval step for care.
States would have to keep paying into the program an amount equal to what they spent on Medicaid in 1991, adjusted for inflation, and residents of states that do not pay would lose eligibility.
The bill relies on Medicare's existing payment and administration structure, including the same deductibles-replacement and DRG hospital payment rules, rather than building a new delivery system.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is universal coverage with strong protections for children, pregnant women, and the poor, and an end to balance billing. The cost is real and broad: a new tax on nearly every taxpayer, employer, and corporation at a time of large deficits, plus continued cost-sharing for most adults. The design is more incremental than a pure single-payer plan, since it reuses Medicare machinery and preserves supplemental employer benefits, but the new taxes would have been the central political obstacle.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and their health subcommittees on the day it was introduced, neither committee ever took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Pete Stark introduced the bill on January 24, 1991, and it was referred the same day to both the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce Committees.
On January 31 it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health, and on February 11 to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and the Environment.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed; the last recorded action is the February 1991 subcommittee referral.
The bill gained sponsors over its two years, including Nancy Pelosi, Barbara Boxer, and Richard Gephardt, but never reached a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, corporations, and private insurers are better off because the bill died: they avoided the new payroll, corporate, and income taxes and kept the existing employer-based insurance system. Americans without health coverage gained nothing.

for.name: Fortney Pete Stark
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-CA), bill sponsor and chair of the Ways and Means Health Subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Mediplan bill and gathered additional sponsors over two years.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor listed in the record is a House Democrat; no Republican supported the bill and it never reached a vote, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.note: Mediplan would replace private primary coverage for most Americans with a public Medicare-style plan, leaving employer plans only as supplemental coverage, and payments would go through Medicare-style carriers on an assignment basis. The industry's survival depended on the bill failing.

The bill imposes a new payroll tax of 40 cents per hour or 10% of wages per employee (capped at $800), and ends employers' role as the source of basic health coverage for workers. Many currently cover employees' insurance, so the tax partially replaces an existing cost, but it is still a new mandate.

A new 2% tax on alternative minimum taxable income would apply to every non-individual taxpayer, including nonprofits on their investment income. This is a direct transfer from corporate balance sheets to the health trust fund.

They would gain tens of millions of newly insured paying patients, but be paid at Medicare rates with mandatory assignment (no balance billing), a 5% bonus for early prenatal care, and a 5% payment cut on cesarean deliveries. Net effect depends on how much uncompensated care they currently absorb.

Coverage of outpatient prescription drugs for children and the poor would create new paying demand, but the Secretary would set a prospective payment methodology (a government-set price approach) rather than paying market charges.
